Work in a classical Cartesian inertial frame with SI units on a fixed open spatial region $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ and time interval $(0,T_f)$, where $T_f>0$ is measured in seconds. Write $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ for functions whose absolute value is integrable on every compact subset. Let all fields be measurable functions of $(t,x)$ on $\Omega\times(0,T_f)$. Require $T>0$ almost everywhere wherever $q/T$ or $r/T$ is used. Let $\rho\ge0$ be mass density in kilograms per cubic metre, $u$ velocity in metres per second, $\sigma$ Cauchy stress in pascals, $b$ body acceleration in metres per second squared, $e$ specific internal energy in joules per kilogram, $q$ outward-positive conductive heat flux in watts per square metre, $r$ specific heat supply in watts per kilogram, $T>0$ absolute temperature in kelvins, and $s$ specific entropy in joules per kilogram kelvin. Set $E:=e+|u|^2/2$, use $t=\sigma n$ for traction and rowwise matrix divergence, and define the test-gradient by $(\nabla\psi)_{ij}:=\partial_{x_j}\psi_i$ and the Frobenius product by $A:B:=\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}B_{ij}$.

A test function is a $C^1$ function on $\Omega\times[0,T_f)$, compactly supported in space-time and vanishing near $T_f$; it may be nonzero at $t=0$. Let scalar test functions be $\phi,\eta,\zeta$ and vector test function be $\psi$. Adopt as a separate weak-branch model assumption that the displayed conservative variables, fluxes and sources below belong to $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and satisfy the following identities for every indicated test function. Initial conservative data $\rho_0,m_0,\mathcal E_0,S_0\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ represent initial mass, momentum, total-energy and entropy densities; the initial terms specify distributional data and do not assert a strong trace.

Mass balance, for every scalar $\phi$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho\,\partial_t\phi+\rho u\cdot\nabla\phi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega\rho_0\phi(0,x)\,dx=0.$$

Momentum balance, for every vector $\psi$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho u\cdot\partial_t\psi+(\rho u\otimes u-\sigma):\nabla\psi+\rho b\cdot\psi\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega m_0\cdot\psi(0,x)\,dx=0.$$

Total-energy balance, for every scalar $\eta$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho E\,\partial_t\eta+(\rho E u-\sigma^{\mathsf T}u+q)\cdot\nabla\eta+(\rho b\cdot u+\rho r)\eta\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega\mathcal E_0\eta(0,x)\,dx=0.$$

Physical entropy inequality, for every nonnegative scalar $\zeta\ge0$,

$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\bigl(\rho s\,\partial_t\zeta+(\rho s u+q/T)\cdot\nabla\zeta+(\rho r/T)\zeta\bigr)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega S_0\zeta(0,x)\,dx\le0.$$

Every conservative density, product, flux and source displayed in these tests is required to be locally integrable up to $t=0$, including $\rho u\otimes u$, $\rho E u$, $\sigma^{\mathsf T}u$, $q/T$ and $\rho r/T$: its absolute value has finite integral on every compact subset of $\Omega\times[0,T_f)$ in the relative topology, using its values for $t>0$. This condition assigns no point values at $t=0$ and asserts no strong initial trace. Interior test functions impose no boundary condition; walls, thermal exchange, periodic identifications and stronger initial trace conditions are separate data. This weak mass/momentum/energy adoption and the physical entropy inequality are not inferred for arbitrary discontinuous or vacuum states from the smooth balance postulate. The source term and the sign of the entropy inequality use the outward-positive heat-flux convention above.

Use a nonrelativistic Cartesian inertial frame with absolute time and SI units. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an open spatial interval measured in metres, let $T_f>0$ be a final time measured in seconds, and let the space-time domain be $\Omega\times(0,T_f)$. The measurable fields are mass density $\rho:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to(0,\infty)$ in kilograms per cubic metre, velocity $u:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to\mathbb R$ in metres per second, specific entropy $s:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to\mathbb R$ in joules per kilogram kelvin, and absolute temperature $T:\Omega\times(0,T_f)\to(0,\infty)$ in kelvins. Put $v=1/\rho$ in cubic metres per kilogram.

Adopt a local-equilibrium constitutive chart on the open state domain $\mathcal U=(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$ with coordinates $(v,s)$ and a $C^2$ fundamental relation $e:\mathcal U\to\mathbb R$ for specific internal energy in joules per kilogram. Let $c_v>0$ be the specific heat at constant volume and $R>0$ the specific gas constant, each in joules per kilogram kelvin. Set $c_p=c_v+R$ as the specific heat at constant pressure and $\gamma=c_p/c_v=1+R/c_v>1$ as the dimensionless ratio of specific heats. Choose reference values $v_*>0$ in cubic metres per kilogram, $T_*>0$ in kelvins, and $s_*\in\mathbb R$ in joules per kilogram kelvin. Adopt the calorically perfect ideal-gas relation
$$e(v,s)=c_vT_*\left(\frac{v_*}{v}\right)^{\gamma-1}\exp\left(\frac{s-s_*}{c_v}\right),$$
with the conventional additive energy reference for which the specific internal energy is zero at zero temperature. Define thermodynamic temperature and pressure by $T=\partial_s e$ and $p=-\partial_v e$. Direct differentiation gives
$$T=\frac{e}{c_v}>0,\qquad p=(\gamma-1)\frac{e}{v}=(\gamma-1)\rho e=R\rho T>0.$$
At fixed $s$, this relation makes $p$ proportional to $\rho^\gamma$, so $\left.\partial_\rho p\right|_s=\gamma p/\rho$ and the positive isentropic sound speed is $c=\sqrt{\left.\partial_\rho p\right|_s}=\sqrt{\gamma p/\rho}$. Thus $\gamma$ is dimensionless, $c$ has units of metres per second, and $p$ has units of pascals. This is a constant-specific-heat ideal-gas approximation; it is restricted to a regime where that closure is adopted.

Define momentum density $m=\rho u$ in kilograms per square metre second and total energy density $E=\rho(e+u^2/2)$ in joules per cubic metre. For $\gamma>1$, the corresponding numerical state is $U=(\rho,m,E)\in\mathbb R^3$ with
$$\mathcal G_\gamma=\left\{(\rho,m,E):\rho>0,\quad E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}>0\right\},\qquad p(U)=(\gamma-1)\left(E-\frac{m^2}{2\rho}\right).$$
The calorically perfect closure makes this state pressure equal to the thermodynamic pressure above. With $u=m/\rho$, its one-dimensional Euler flux and isentropic sound speed are
$$F(U)=\left(m,\frac{m^2}{\rho}+p(U),u(E+p(U))\right),\qquad c(U)=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma p(U)}{\rho}}.$$
The components of $F$ are mass flux in kilograms per square metre second, momentum flux in pascals, and energy flux in watts per square metre. The speed $c$ is in metres per second.

Adopt the inviscid one-dimensional branch with zero body acceleration, zero specific heat supply, zero conductive heat flux, and isotropic Cauchy stress $-pI$. In this branch, assume the locally integrable conservative variables, fluxes, entropy density, and entropy flux satisfy the following identities in the distributional sense. Let $\rho_0,m_0,E_0,S_0\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ be the initial mass density in kilograms per cubic metre, momentum density in kilograms per square metre second, total energy density in joules per cubic metre, and entropy density in joules per cubic metre kelvin, respectively. Require all displayed densities, fluxes, and products to be locally integrable up to $t=0$: their absolute values have finite integrals on every compact subset of $\Omega\times[0,T_f)$ in the relative topology, using the fields for $t>0$. This requirement assigns no point values at $t=0$ and asserts no strong initial trace. Test functions $\phi,\psi,\eta,\zeta\in C^1(\Omega\times[0,T_f))$ are compactly supported in space-time and vanish near $T_f$; $\zeta$ is nonnegative, and tests may be nonzero at $t=0$. Then adopt
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(\rho\,\partial_t\phi+\rho u\,\partial_x\phi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega\rho_0\phi(0,x)\,dx=0,$$
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(\rho u\,\partial_t\psi+(\rho u^2+p)\partial_x\psi\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega m_0\psi(0,x)\,dx=0,$$
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(E\,\partial_t\eta+u(E+p)\partial_x\eta\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega E_0\eta(0,x)\,dx=0,$$
and
$$\int_0^{T_f}\!\!\int_\Omega\left(\rho s\,\partial_t\zeta+\rho u s\,\partial_x\zeta\right)\,dx\,dt+\int_\Omega S_0\zeta(0,x)\,dx\le0.$$
The last inequality is a separately adopted physical entropy inequality. It is not deduced from the conservative equations or from smooth-flow identities. This postulate specifies a physical model and its idealized local-equilibrium closure; it does not assert existence or uniqueness of a weak solution, prove that actual matter obeys the model, or identify a computed state with an experimental observation.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$: every sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ of nonempty sets admits a function $c$ with $c(n)\in X_n$. Let $T>0$, let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^3$ be a bounded connected $C^2$ domain, let $I$ be an open interval containing $[0,T]$, and let $\rho_0,\nu>0$. Suppose $u,v\in C^1([0,T];C^2(\overline D;\mathbb R^3))$ and $p,q\in C([0,T];C^1(\overline D))$ extend with these regularities to a neighborhood of $\overline D$, with $\operatorname{div}u=\operatorname{div}v=0$. Let $f\in C([0,T]\times\overline D;\mathbb R^3)$, and for any velocity $w$ and scalar pressure $\pi$ set

$$\mathcal R(w,\pi):=\partial_tw+(w\cdot\nabla)w+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla\pi-\nu\Delta w-f.$$

Assume $\mathcal R(u,p)=0$, and suppose $u$ and $v$ have the same boundary trace on $\partial D$ at each time. Define $r=\mathcal R(v,q)$.

the bilinear gradient norm

$$L(t)=\sup_{x\in\overline D}\ \sup_{|\xi|=|\zeta|=1}\left|\zeta\cdot D_xu(t,x)\xi\right|,$$

where $(D_xu)_{ij}=\partial_{x_j}u_i$ is the row-component Jacobian and $\xi,\zeta$ are Euclidean unit vectors. For a vector field $F$, write $\|F\|_{L^2(D)}=(\int_D|F(x)|^2\,dx)^{1/2}$. Set $A(t)=\int_0^tL(s)\,ds$. Then for every $t\in[0,T]$,

$$\|v(t)-u(t)\|_{L^2(D)}\le e^{A(t)}\left(\|v(0)-u(0)\|_{L^2(D)}+\int_0^t e^{-A(s)}\|r(s)\|_{L^2(D)}\,ds\right).$$

The same estimate holds on the flat periodic channel $D_{\rm ch}=\mathbb T_{L_x}\times(0,h)\times\mathbb T_{L_z}$, where $\mathbb T_L=\mathbb R/(L\mathbb Z)$, when the same equations and regularity assumptions hold, norms and integrals are over one periodic cell, and $u,v$ share the two wall traces; paired periodic-face terms cancel. In particular, let $w$ be smooth and divergence-free with traces $\gamma_0(t,x,z)+a(t)e_x$ at $y=0$ and $\gamma_h(t,x,z)+b(t)e_x$ at $y=h$, where $\gamma_0,\gamma_h$ are prescribed wall-velocity fields, while the exact solution $u$ has traces $\gamma_0,\gamma_h$. For $a,b\in C^1([0,T])$, set

$$\ell(t,x,y,z)=\bigl(a(t)(1-y/h)+b(t)y/h,\,0,\,0\bigr),\qquad v=w-\ell.$$

The corrected residual is

$$r_\ell=\mathcal R(v,q)=\mathcal R(w,q)-\ell_t-(\ell\cdot\nabla)w-(w\cdot\nabla)\ell+(\ell\cdot\nabla)\ell+\nu\Delta\ell.$$

Thus $\|w(t)-u(t)\|_2\le\|\ell(t)\|_2+\|v(t)-u(t)\|_2$, with the preceding estimate applied to $v$ and $r_\ell$. This result assumes the displayed lift data and makes no general boundary-lifting claim, Prandtl-profile existence claim, or viscosity-uniform no-slip inviscid-limit claim. In SI units, $[\rho_0]=\mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, $[\nu]=\mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$, $[p]=[q]=\mathrm{Pa}$, $[f]=[r]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, $[a]=[b]=[\ell]=\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, $[h]=\mathrm m$, $L$ has units $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and $A$ is dimensionless. Velocity, error and lift volume $L^2$ norms have units $\mathrm{m^{5/2}\,s^{-1}}$; residual volume $L^2$ norms have units $\mathrm{m^{5/2}\,s^{-2}}$, so their time-integrated contribution has units $\mathrm{m^{5/2}\,s^{-1}}$.

Use a classical Cartesian inertial frame with absolute time $t$ in seconds and horizontal coordinates $x=(x_1,x_2)$ in metres, with upward vertical coordinate $z$ in metres; let $e_z$ be the upward unit vector. Fix horizontal periods $L_1,L_2>0$ metres and identify opposite horizontal faces by translations, so the horizontal cell is the quotient torus $\mathbb T^2_L:=\mathbb R^2/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z)$. Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be a nonempty open time interval and let $h>0$ metres. The flat reference liquid region is $\Omega_0:=\mathbb T^2_L\times(-h,0)$; the bottom $z=-h$ is a fixed solid bed and the upper interface is the graph $z=\eta(x,t)$, where $\eta:\mathbb T^2_L\times I\to\mathbb R$ is the surface displacement in metres. Horizontal periodic faces are mathematical identifications, not physical walls.

Adopt a homogeneous single-component liquid with constant mass density $\rho>0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, constant downward gravitational acceleration $-g e_z$ with $g>0$ in metres per second squared, and constant surface-tension coefficient $\gamma>0$ in newtons per metre, equivalently kilograms per second squared. The gas above the liquid is modeled only by constant pressure $p_a$ in pascals; no gas momentum equation is included. Let $p_\ell$ denote the liquid pressure in pascals. This model assumes a horizontally periodic scalar velocity potential $\phi$ in metres squared per second, defined on $\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I$; the fluid velocity is the vector field $u:=\nabla\phi:\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I\to\mathbb R^3$ in metres per second, with no additive uniform component. The model is inviscid, meaning no viscous-stress or viscous-dissipation terms are included; it is incompressible and irrotational, meaning $\operatorname{div}u=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}u=0$. On the torus this potential assumption is stronger than irrotationality alone, since a curl-free field need not be the gradient of a periodic scalar. Assume $\phi$ is at least $C^3$ and $\eta$ is at least $C^2$; derivatives below are classical.

The outward unit normal from liquid to gas on the graph is $n=(-\nabla_h\eta,1)/\sqrt{1+|\nabla_h\eta|^2}$, where $\nabla_h:=(\partial_{x_1},\partial_{x_2})$ and $\Delta_h:=\partial_{x_1}^2+\partial_{x_2}^2$. Define the signed curvature of this graph by $\kappa:=-\nabla_h\cdot(\nabla_h\eta/\sqrt{1+|\nabla_h\eta|^2})$; with the stated upward normal its first-order value about the flat state is $-\Delta_h\eta$, and $\kappa$ has units of inverse metres. Adopt the liquid-minus-gas pressure jump $p_\ell-p_a=\gamma\kappa$. At the fixed bed impose only impermeability, meaning zero normal fluid velocity, $u_z=0$, equivalently $\phi_z=0$ at $z=-h$; no-slip is not imposed in this inviscid branch. The upper boundary moves with the fluid and obeys the explicit first-order kinematic equation below; it is not a solid wall.

The selected first-order model is defined by retaining only terms linear in perturbations about the hydrostatic rest state $\eta=0$, $u=0$, and $p_\ell=p_a-\rho g z$, then evaluating surface derivatives at $z=0$. Products of perturbations are discarded, with no error estimate for replacing a finite-amplitude flow by this linear model. On $\Omega_0\times I$ the adopted equations and boundary conditions are

$$\Delta_h\phi+\partial_z^2\phi=0,\qquad -h<z<0,$$

$$\partial_z\phi(x,-h,t)=0,$$

$$\partial_t\eta(x,t)=\partial_z\phi(x,0,t),\qquad \partial_t\phi(x,0,t)+g\eta(x,t)-\frac{\gamma}{\rho}\Delta_h\eta(x,t)=0.$$

These are model assumptions for the stated idealized regime. They assert no existence or uniqueness for the nonlinear free-boundary equations, no finite-amplitude approximation bound, and no empirical claim that a particular liquid satisfies this model.

Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be nonempty and open, $h>0$ metres, and $L_1,L_2>0$ metres. Set $\mathbb T^2_L:=\mathbb R^2/(L_1\mathbb Z\times L_2\mathbb Z)$, with horizontal coordinate $x\in\mathbb T^2_L$ in metres, vertical coordinate $z\in[-h,0]$ in metres, and absolute time $t\in I$ in seconds. Let $\rho>0$ be constant liquid mass density in kilograms per cubic metre, $g>0$ downward gravitational acceleration magnitude in metres per second squared, and $\gamma>0$ constant surface tension in newtons per metre. Let $\phi:\mathbb T^2_L\times[-h,0]\times I\to\mathbb R$ and $\eta:\mathbb T^2_L\times I\to\mathbb R$ be the first-order fields, with units metres squared per second and metres respectively, satisfying

$$\Delta_h\phi+\partial_z^2\phi=0,\quad \partial_z\phi(x,-h,t)=0,$$

$$\partial_t\eta(x,t)=\partial_z\phi(x,0,t),\quad \partial_t\phi(x,0,t)+g\eta(x,t)-\frac{\gamma}{\rho}\Delta_h\eta(x,t)=0,$$

where $\Delta_h:=\partial_{x_1}^2+\partial_{x_2}^2$. For any $m=(m_1,m_2)\in\mathbb Z^2\setminus\{(0,0)\}$ define the wavevector $\mathbf k:=2\pi(m_1/L_1,m_2/L_2)$ in inverse metres and $k:=|\mathbf k|>0$. Let $i\in\mathbb C$ satisfy $i^2=-1$. A complex mode of angular frequency $\omega\in\mathbb C$ in inverse seconds is a pair $\eta_c(x,t)=H e^{i(\mathbf k\cdot x-\omega t)}$ and $\phi_c(x,z,t)=F(z)e^{i(\mathbf k\cdot x-\omega t)}$, with $H\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$ in metres and $F\in C^2([-h,0],\mathbb C)$ in metres squared per second; its real and imaginary parts are real-valued model fields. Such a nonzero mode exists exactly when

$$\omega^2=\left(gk+\frac{\gamma}{\rho}k^3\right)\tanh(kh),$$

and each of the two frequencies $\omega=\pm\sqrt{(gk+(\gamma/\rho)k^3)\tanh(kh)}$ admits a nonzero mode. Here $\tanh s:=\sinh(s)/\cosh(s)$. This is a conditional prediction of the stated first-order model, not a measurement or a claim that any actual fluid realizes every assumption.

The radicand is positive; the identity $|y_\delta(t+h)-y_\delta(t)|=|Y(t+h)-Y(t)|/(y_\delta(t+h)+y_\delta(t))$ first gives continuity of $y_\delta$, and the same difference-of-squares identity in the difference quotient gives $y_\delta'=Y'/(2y_\delta)$. Dropping the nonnegative diffusion term in step 1.2 and using $Y/y_\delta\le y_\delta$ and $\sqrt{Y}/y_\delta\le1$ yields $y_\delta'\le L y_\delta+R$. The function $L$ is continuous because $\overline D$ is compact and $D_xu$ is continuous; for $A(t)=\int_0^tL(s)\,ds$, the difference quotient is the average of $L$ on the interval between $t$ and $t+h$, so continuity gives $A'=L$.
